function.name: generate_image_tool
function.description: Generates an image based on the provided description and saves it with the specified file name. The image description should be detailed to ensure the resulting image matches the desired subject and surroundings; otherwise, these aspects will be chosen randomly. This function is not intended for generating images from textual data. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

desc.description: A single string that provides a detailed description of the desired image. For example, 'a sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground'.

file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

function.name: tts_tool
function.description: Converts the provided text content to speech and saves the resulting audio to a file. This function is intended for voice narration and should be used accordingly. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The text content that needs to be converted to speech.

speaker.description: The voice to be used for the text-to-speech conversion.

file_name.description: The name of the file to save the audio output without the extension. If left empty, a default name will be generated based on the content.

function.name: write_markdown_tool
function.description: Writes the provided content to a Markdown (.md) file on the disk. This function should be used when there is a need to persist text data in Markdown format as a result of a user action or a process that requires saving information in a structured text file. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The Markdown formatted text content to be written to the file.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the Markdown content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.name: write_html_tool
function.description: Writes an HTML file to disk with the given content. Ensures HTML tags within the content are properly closed. This function should be used when there is a need to save HTML content to a file as part of a 'save' operation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.name: search_web_tool
function.description: Executes a search query using the DuckDuckGo search engine and returns a specified number of search results from a given source. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

user_agent.description: The User-Agent string to be used for the HTTP request to simulate a particular browser, which is optional. Some websites may require this for access.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** that shows how to create a Google Cloud Compute Engine instance that:

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| **Operating system** | Ubuntu 20.04 LTS (Focal) |
| **GPU** | NVIDIA RTX A6000 (if available; otherwise use the closest supported GPU such as `nvidia-tesla-a100`) |
| **Machine type** | Custom machine with 8 vCPU / 32 GB RAM (adjust as needed) |
| **Zone** | `us-central1-a` (pick a zone that supports GPUs) |
| **Project** | `<YOUR_PROJECT_ID>` |

> ⚠️ **Important** – Google Cloud does **not** use the “EC2” terminology; it’s called **Compute Engine**.  
> The RTX A6000 is not listed in the public GPU catalog, so you’ll likely need to use `nvidia-tesla-a100` or another supported GPU. If you truly need an RTX A6000, you’ll have to check the latest GPU catalog or contact Google support.

---

## 1. Prerequisites

1. **Enable the Compute Engine API**  
   ```bash
   gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com
   ```

2. **Create a service account** (or use your own credentials) and download its key.  
   ```bash
   gcloud iam service-accounts create gce-installer \
       --display-name="GCE Installer"
   gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding <YOUR_PROJECT_ID> \
       --member="serviceAccount:gce-installer@<YOUR_PROJECT_ID>.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
       --role="roles/compute.admin"
   gcloud iam service-accounts keys create ~/gce-installer-key.json \
       --iam-account=gce-installer@<YOUR_PROJECT_ID>.iam.gserviceaccount.com
   ```

3. **Authenticate** (replace the path with where you stored the key)  
   ```bash
   gcloud auth activate-service-account --key-file=~/gce-installer-key.json
   ```

4. **Set the default project & zone**  
   ```bash
   gcloud config set project <YOUR_PROJECT_ID>
   gcloud config set compute/zone us-central1-a
   ```

---

## 2. Create the Instance with `gcloud`

```bash
gcloud compute instances create my-ubuntu-gpu-instance \
    --machine-type=n1-standard-8 \
    --image-family=ubuntu-2004-lts \
    --image-project=ubuntu-os-cloud \
    --boot-disk-size=200GB \
    --boot-disk-type=pd-ssd \
    --accelerator=type=nvidia-tesla-a100,count=1 \
    --maintenance-policy=MIGRATE \
    --restart-on-failure \
    --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh \
    --tags=http-server,https-server
```

### Explanation of the flags

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--machine-type=n1-standard-8` | 8 vCPU, 30 GB RAM (adjust to your needs) |
| `--image-family=ubuntu-2004-lts` | Latest Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image |
| `--image-project=ubuntu-os-cloud` | Official Ubuntu image repository |
| `--boot-disk-size=200GB` | Size of the boot disk |
| `--boot-disk-type=pd-ssd` | SSD persistent disk |
| `--accelerator=type=nvidia-tesla-a100,count=1` | Attach one RTX A6000‑equivalent GPU |
| `--maintenance-policy=MIGRATE` | VM will be live‑migrated during maintenance |
| `--restart-on-failure` | Auto‑restart if the VM crashes |
| `--metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh` | Optional startup script (e.g., install drivers) |
| `--tags=http-server,https-server` | Allow HTTP/HTTPS traffic (for firewall rules) |

> **Tip:** If you need a different GPU, replace `nvidia-tesla-a100` with the GPU type you want (e.g., `nvidia-tesla-v100`).  
> You can list all available GPUs in a zone with:
> ```bash
> gcloud compute accelerator-types list --zone us-central1-a
> ```

---

## 3. Create the Instance with the REST API (curl)

If you prefer to use the raw REST API, here’s a **curl** example that sends a signed JWT (you’ll need to replace placeholders with real values).

```bash
# 1. Generate an OAuth 2.0 access token (using the service account key)
ACCESS_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)

# 2. Build the JSON payload
cat <<EOF > instance.json
{
  "name": "my-ubuntu-gpu-instance",
  "machineType": "zones/us-central1-a/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 200,
        "diskType": "zones/us-central1-a/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        { "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "accelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "zones/us-central1-a/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a100"
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\nsudo apt-get update\nsudo apt-get install -y cuda-drivers"
      }
    ]
  }
}
EOF

# 3. Send the POST request
curl -X POST \
  "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/<YOUR_PROJECT_ID>/zones/us-central1-a/instances" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @instance.json
```

### What the JSON does

- **`name`** – Instance name.
- **`machineType`** – Full URL to the machine type.
- **`disks`** – Boot disk configuration (Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, 200 GB SSD).
- **`networkInterfaces`** – Default network + external IP.
- **`accelerators`** – Attach one GPU.
- **`metadata`** – Optional startup script (install CUDA drivers, etc.).

---

## 4. Verify the Instance

After the command finishes, you can check the instance status:

```bash
gcloud compute instances describe my-ubuntu-gpu-instance
```

Look for:

- `status: RUNNING`
- `guestAccelerators` section showing the GPU type and count.
- `disks` section confirming the boot disk size/type.

---

## 5. Clean Up (Optional)

When you’re done, delete the instance to avoid incurring charges:

```bash
gcloud compute instances delete my-ubuntu-gpu-instance --quiet
```

---

### Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `gcloud compute instances create ...` | Creates the VM via CLI |
| `curl -X POST ...` | Creates the VM via REST API |
| `gcloud compute instances describe ...` | Shows instance details |
| `gcloud compute instances delete ...` | Deletes the instance |

Feel free to tweak the machine type, GPU count, disk size, or region to match your workload. Happy computing!
